lessons.title: Above treeline
lessons.objective: You can explain the exposure and shelter changes above treeline.

payload.prompt: What changes most when the trees stop at treeline?

options.text: Shelter from wind, rain and lightning mostly disappears
options.explanation: Trees break the wind and give a little cover. Above them the whole sky and every gust are yours.

options.text: It gets warmer because you are closer to the sun
options.explanation: Air cools as you climb, and wind makes it feel colder. Being closer to the sun does not warm the air.

options.text: The trail always gets easier to follow
options.explanation: Bare rock, talus and snow often hide the tread, so route finding usually gets harder, not easier.

options.text: Phone signal gets reliable because nothing blocks it
options.explanation: Coverage in the mountains is patchy. Never count on a signal as part of your plan.

explanation.correct: Treeline is where shelter ends. Above it you get more wind, colder air, stronger sun and nowhere to duck when weather turns.
explanation.incorrect: Think about what a forest gives you: wind break, shade and cover. Above treeline all of that is gone, so weather hits harder and faster.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Once we're above treeline, there's no hiding from the weather."

payload.prompt: You reach treeline at 10:30 AM. The sky is changing. Now what?

situation.narrative: You and a friend are on a high-country trail. The last stunted trees are just ahead, then a long open ridge to a lake. Wind is picking up and small clouds are starting to stack to the west.

facts.label: Ahead
facts.value: 2 miles of open ridge, no cover

options.label: Turn around here and enjoy the lower forest lakes instead
options.consequence: You lose the ridge view but keep all your options. Clouds that build this early can turn into thunderstorms before noon.
considerations: Treeline is the last easy place to change your mind.
Building clouds plus rising wind is a reason to turn early, not a reason to hurry across.

options.label: Wait at treeline for 20 minutes, then decide with a clear look at the sky
options.consequence: A short, disciplined pause can be reasonable if you decide a turn-back rule first. Do not drift onto the ridge because it looks a bit better.
considerations: Set the rule before you wait, such as 'if clouds darken, we go down.'
Wait below the open ridge, not on it.

options.label: Hurry across the ridge to the lake before it changes
options.consequence: You would be the tallest thing on two miles of open ridge when storms build. Hurrying also invites slips on rocky ground.
considerations: Speed does not protect you from lightning.
A bad forecast plus no cover is exactly when to avoid a ridge.

options.label: Send the faster hiker ahead to check the ridge while the other waits
options.consequence: Splitting up puts one person alone in the most exposed spot with no help nearby if weather or a fall goes wrong.
considerations: Groups make decisions together and stay together.
Scouting ahead in building weather adds risk without adding information.

payload.expertNote: Experienced high-country hikers treat treeline as a checkpoint: look at the sky, the time and the group, and be willing to turn around right there.
payload.sayThisLine: "Let's make the call at treeline, not out on the ridge."
payload.safetyNote: Follow official land manager guidance and check the mountain forecast. Swoon'd teaches appreciation, not survival training.

payload.prompt: Match each high-country word to what it means:

pairs.definition: The elevation above which trees stop growing
Stunted, wind-twisted trees at the edge of treeline
Steep drop-offs beside the route where a fall would be serious
Slopes of loose, tumbled rock that shift underfoot

explanation.summary: Treeline and krummholz tell you the shelter is ending. Exposure and talus tell you how the ground and the drop-offs will feel once you are up there.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The krummholz is our cue that treeline is close."

payload.prompt: Your friend freezes on a narrow section with a big drop. Push on?

scene.alt: A hiker standing very still on a narrow rocky ridge trail, with a steep drop-off falling away on one side.

explanation.correct: Fear on an exposed section is useful information. Stop somewhere stable, calm the pace, and be willing to turn back rather than force someone across a place where a fall is serious.
explanation.incorrect: Pushing a frozen person along an exposed edge raises the risk of a fall. Pause on stable ground, check how she feels, and choose to go back if she is not comfortable.
explanation.sayThisLine: "No rush. If this section feels wrong, we turn around."

payload.ruleTag: Exposure is a real reason to turn

payload.prompt: Trailhead is 70 F. Treeline is 3,000 ft higher. Guess the air temp.

explanation.correct: Air cools roughly 3 to 5 F for every 1,000 ft you climb, so about 10 to 15 degrees over 3,000 ft. That is before wind chill, which can make it feel colder still.
explanation.incorrect: A rule of thumb is 3 to 5 F cooler per 1,000 ft of climbing. Over 3,000 ft that is about 10 to 15 degrees, and wind above treeline can make it feel colder.
explanation.sayThisLine: "It'll be about ten degrees colder up there, and windier."

lessons.title: Storm-proofing your day
lessons.objective: You can schedule a high route around storms.

payload.prompt: You are planning a peak day in July. What schedule do you set?

situation.narrative: The peak has a long, open summit ridge. In summer, afternoon thunderstorms are common in the range. Your friend prefers a slow breakfast and a late start.

options.label: Start before dawn, set a noon turnaround, and be off the ridge by then
options.consequence: You climb in the cool, still morning and are heading down before storms usually build. The noon rule holds even if the summit is close.
considerations: The clock decides, not how close the top looks.
Being off exposed terrain early is the whole point of an alpine start.

options.label: Start at 8 AM and turn around if clouds build
options.consequence: Watching the sky is good, but a late start leaves you high when storms form, and clouds can build fast. You would have little cushion.
considerations: A sky-based rule still needs a hard clock behind it.
Pick an easier objective if you cannot start early.

options.label: Start at 11 AM after a long breakfast and move fast
options.consequence: You would reach the exposed ridge exactly when storms are most likely. Moving fast does not shorten how long you are up there.
considerations: Late starts put you on the ridge in the riskiest hours.
Speed is not a safety plan.

options.label: Go whenever, because the forecast said only a 20 percent chance
options.consequence: A low chance is not zero, and mountain storms can be very local. A ridge is the worst place to find out.
considerations: Recheck the mountain forecast the morning of, and again on the trail.
Even small chances matter when there is no shelter.

payload.expertNote: The alpine start is not about toughness. It is about buying a cushion before the afternoon convection builds, and about agreeing to a turnaround before anyone is tired.
payload.sayThisLine: "We start at four and we're off the summit by noon."
payload.safetyNote: Check the current mountain forecast and follow official guidance. No time-based plan replaces watching the sky.

payload.prompt: Put a storm-aware high route day in order:

items.text: The night before, check the mountain forecast and set a turnaround time
items.why: Deciding your rules before you are tired or excited makes them easier to keep.

items.text: Start hiking before dawn with a headlamp
items.why: Climbing early puts you on high ground during the calm morning hours.

items.text: Reach the high point or the turnaround, whichever comes first
items.why: The turnaround is a ceiling. If you reach it first, the goal can wait for another day.

items.text: Head down and be below treeline or off the ridge by noon
items.why: Afternoon storms usually build after midday, so you want to be off exposed ground by then.

items.text: Check in with your contact once you are back
items.why: It closes the loop so nobody starts a search you do not need.

explanation.correct: Plan and set the clock, start early, honor the turnaround, get down before storms usually form, then check in. Each step protects the next one.
explanation.incorrect: Set your rules the night before, start early, turn at the first of goal or clock, be off the ridge by midday, then tell your contact you are safe.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Forecast, early start, turnaround, down by noon, check in."

payload.prompt: You hear distant thunder 20 minutes below the summit. Continue up?

scene.alt: A hiker on an open alpine slope looking up at a summit while dark clouds build beyond the ridge.

explanation.correct: If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Leave summits and ridges right away and head down toward lower, more sheltered ground while you still have time.
explanation.incorrect: Thunder means lightning is near enough to be a threat, roughly 10 miles or closer. Going up puts you on the highest, most exposed ground. Turn around and go down now.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I heard thunder. Summit's off, we're heading down."

payload.prompt: Complete the lightning rules for the high country:
payload.template: No place outdoors is truly safe, so leave {{place}} early. Avoid lone trees, and wait {{wait}} after the last thunder.

explanation.correct: High, open, exposed places are the most dangerous in a storm, so leave them early. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder, because lightning can strike well after the rain seems to have passed.
explanation.incorrect: Ridges and summits are the highest, most exposed spots, so leave them before storms arrive. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back up, and avoid lone trees.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Thirty minutes after the last thunder, not thirty seconds."

payload.prompt: A storm catches your group of four on an open slope. Best move?

options.text: Get off the ridge and away from high points, spread out about 50 feet apart, and keep descending
options.explanation: Moving toward lower ground and spacing out means one strike is less likely to hurt everyone.

options.text: Huddle together under a single tall tree for cover
options.explanation: A lone tall tree is a lightning target, and a huddle puts everyone in one danger zone.

options.text: Finish the last few hundred feet to the summit first
options.explanation: The summit is the highest, most exposed point, exactly where you do not want to be in a storm.

options.text: Sit down on the ridge crest and wait it out
options.explanation: Sitting still on a crest keeps you at the most exposed place instead of leaving it.

explanation.correct: No outdoor spot is safe, but getting away from ridges, high points and lone trees and spreading the group out lowers the risk. Keep moving down toward lower, more sheltered ground.
explanation.incorrect: Avoid the highest ground, lone trees and clumps of people. Move down and away from ridges, spread out about 50 feet, and keep heading to lower ground.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Spread out and keep dropping. Nobody stops on the ridge."

lessons.title: Late snow and traction
lessons.objective: You can judge when snow needs traction or a turn.

payload.prompt: A steep, hard snowfield covers the trail near the pass. What do you do?

situation.narrative: It is early July and a trail report mentions lingering snow. Ahead, the trail crosses a steep, firm snow slope for about 200 feet. Below it, the slope runs out onto rocks. You have trail shoes and poles only.

options.label: Turn back or choose a route without the steep snow crossing
options.consequence: A slip on steep, hard snow can become an uncontrolled slide into rocks. Without traction and training, skipping it is the right call.
considerations: Ordinary hikers are not equipped to stop a slide on steep firm snow.
The pass will still be there when the snow has melted or you have skills.

options.label: Check with the land manager and come back after it melts or with training
options.consequence: This is patient and sensible. Current trail reports tell you when traction, skills or gear are needed and when the crossing has softened or melted.
considerations: Recent reports beat old ones.
Learn snow skills from a qualified course, not from a video.

options.label: Cross carefully, using your poles for balance
options.consequence: Poles do not arrest a slide. On a steep, firm slope with rocks below, a small slip can have very serious consequences.
considerations: Careful is not the same as equipped.
The consequences of the fall matter more than how confident you feel.

options.label: Follow the boot prints of the hikers who crossed before you
options.consequence: Old footsteps can freeze into slick steps or lead to a bad line. Someone else's crossing does not prove yours is safe.
considerations: Tracks show where people went, not that the snow is safe.
Conditions change through the day.

payload.expertNote: Microspikes help on packed snow and icy trail. Steep, hard snow with a bad runout calls for training, an ice axe and often crampons, which is a different skill set from hiking.
payload.sayThisLine: "That crossing's steeper than I have the gear or skills for. Let's turn."
payload.safetyNote: Follow official land manager guidance. Learn snow travel and self-arrest from a qualified course before crossing steep snow.

payload.prompt: When are microspikes the right tool?

options.text: Packed snow or icy patches on a gentle to moderate trail
options.explanation: This is what microspikes are built for: extra grip on packed snow and ice on ordinary hiking terrain.

options.text: Steep, hard snow slopes with a serious runout below
options.explanation: That terrain calls for training, ice axe and often crampons. Microspikes are not made for it.

options.text: Dry, rocky trail on a warm afternoon
options.explanation: On bare rock, spikes are awkward, slippery and can damage the surface. Leave them in the pack.

options.text: Deep, soft snow where you sink to the knee
options.explanation: Spikes do not stop you from sinking. Snowshoes or waiting for firmer snow are the answer there.

explanation.correct: Microspikes add grip on packed snow and ice on ordinary trails. They do not turn you into a mountaineer, and they are not made for steep hard snow or bare rock.
explanation.incorrect: Microspikes are for packed snow and icy trail. Steep hard snow needs training and different gear, and on bare rock or deep soft snow they do not help.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Microspikes for the icy trail, not for the steep snow slope."

payload.prompt: It is 2 PM and you are sinking to the knee with every step. Best plan?

scene.alt: A hiker sinking deep into soft afternoon snow on a sunny slope, leaving a line of knee-deep holes behind.

choices.label: Turn back; go earlier next time

explanation.correct: Afternoon sun turns snow soft, and postholing is slow, exhausting and can twist a knee or ankle. Snow is often firmer in the cool morning, so an earlier start makes a big difference.
explanation.incorrect: Wading through soft snow drains your energy and slows you down, which shrinks your daylight and storm margin. Turn back and try again earlier when the snow is firmer.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The snow's mush by afternoon. Let's start earlier next time."

payload.ruleTag: Soft snow: earlier or turn back

payload.prompt: Match each snow term to its meaning:

pairs.definition: Accumulated snow that lingers on high trails into summer
Slip-on traction for packed snow and icy trail
Sinking deeply into soft snow with each step
The ground below a slope where you would end up if you slid

explanation.summary: Snowpack is what stays; microspikes help on gentle packed snow and ice; postholing is what soft afternoon snow does to your legs; and the runout is what tells you if a slip would be a problem.
explanation.sayThisLine: "What's the runout if someone slips on that snow?"

payload.prompt: Finish the late-snow planning sentence:
payload.template: Check a recent {{source}} before you go, and start {{when}} when the snow is firmer.

explanation.correct: A recent trail report tells you where snow still lingers and whether it needs traction. Snow is usually firmest in the early morning and softens as the day warms.
explanation.incorrect: Use a recent trail report to learn what the snow is doing, and start early, because snow softens through the day and becomes exhausting to walk on.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Let's check the latest trail report and start early for firm snow."

lessons.title: Avalanche awareness
lessons.objective: You can read a danger rating and know awareness is not training.

payload.prompt: The avalanche forecast says Considerable. What does that tell you?

options.text: Dangerous conditions: avalanches are likely on steep slopes, so avoid avalanche terrain unless trained
options.explanation: Considerable is level 3 of 5. Human-triggered avalanches are likely on steep slopes, and it is a serious rating.

options.text: A middle-of-the-road day, so most hikers can relax
options.explanation: Middle of the scale does not mean mild. Level 3 is where most avalanche accidents happen.

options.text: Mostly safe, with only tiny slides on rare steep spots
options.explanation: That describes a much lower rating. Considerable is a step above Moderate and is a warning sign.

options.text: Avalanches are only a risk in winter, so it does not affect summer hiking
options.explanation: Snow can linger on high slopes well into summer, and forecasts are only issued when centers are active.

explanation.correct: The scale runs 1 Low, 2 Moderate, 3 Considerable, 4 High, 5 Extreme. Considerable means dangerous conditions where human-triggered avalanches are likely. Without training, avoid steep snow slopes.
explanation.incorrect: Considerable is level 3 of 5 and a serious rating. Read the forecast from your local avalanche center and stay out of avalanche terrain unless you have real training.
explanation.sayThisLine: "It's Considerable today. That's a hard pass on the steep snow."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: The avalanche center has it at Considerable above treeline, so we're skipping the couloir and sticking to the low trail.

payload.question: What is she doing?

options.text: Reading the danger rating and choosing terrain to match
options.explanation: Yes. She checked the forecast and picked a lower-risk route because the rating was high.

options.text: Choosing gear for a snowy summit push
options.explanation: She is skipping the steep snow entirely, not gearing up for it.

options.text: Bragging that she took an avalanche course
options.explanation: Nothing she said is about training. She is applying the forecast to a terrain choice.

options.text: Guessing the weather from the clouds
options.explanation: She named the avalanche center's forecast. That is data, not a guess.

payload.translation: She checked the official avalanche forecast, saw a serious danger rating, and chose a route that stays out of steep avalanche terrain.

followUps.line: Which avalanche center do you check for your area?
followUps.why: It shows you know forecasts come from local centers, and invites her to share her habits.

followUps.line: Have you taken an avalanche course?
followUps.why: It respects the training side of the topic and opens a real conversation.

payload.prompt: The forecast is High. A shortcut climbs a steep, snowy bowl. What now?

situation.narrative: It is a spring day on a high route. The avalanche forecast reads High. You have no avalanche training or rescue gear. A steep, snow-filled bowl offers a short cut, and you can see old slide debris at its base.

options.label: Avoid the bowl and all steep snow; take a lower, gentler route or turn back
options.consequence: You skip the risk entirely. At a High rating, even trained people avoid avalanche terrain.
considerations: Old debris is evidence that slides run here.
A shortcut is never worth the exposure.

options.label: Go home and plan a different, lower hike for today
options.consequence: This is conservative and sensible. The mountain will be there when the rating drops and you have a route without avalanche terrain.
considerations: Changing objectives is a normal part of mountain plans.
Learning avalanche skills is the next step if you want steeper snow.

options.label: Cross one at a time, so only one person is at risk
options.consequence: Crossing one at a time only helps trained groups with rescue gear. Without training or gear, the one crossing is alone and the others cannot rescue.
considerations: Rescue skills are what make spacing useful.
Untrained spacing is not a safety system.

options.label: Cross quickly since the snow looks stable
options.consequence: You cannot judge snow stability by looking. Slopes can look calm and still release under one person's weight.
considerations: Most avalanche victims trigger the slide themselves.
Speed does not lower the risk.

payload.expertNote: Awareness is not training. It gives you the vocabulary to read a forecast and know when to stay out. If you want to travel in avalanche terrain, take a hands-on course from a qualified provider.
payload.sayThisLine: "High danger and no training means we stay off the steep snow."
payload.safetyNote: Take a real avalanche course before entering avalanche terrain, and check avalanche.org for your local forecast. This lesson is awareness, not training.

payload.prompt: A snowy ridge edge looks like a great photo spot. Step out on it?

scene.alt: A windswept ridge crest where a smooth shelf of snow overhangs the drop on the sheltered side.

explanation.correct: A cornice is an overhanging shelf of wind-packed snow. It can break off farther back from the edge than you expect, and you cannot tell by looking where the solid ground ends.
explanation.incorrect: The edge may be a cornice, and it could collapse under your weight, sending you down the far side. Stay well back from ridge edges with snow.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Stay back from that edge. It could be a cornice."

payload.prompt: Match each danger rating to its number on the 1 to 5 scale:

explanation.summary: The scale runs Low, Moderate, Considerable, High, Extreme. Real avalanche training teaches what each level means for terrain choices. Check your local avalanche center's forecast before you go.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Level three is Considerable, and that's already serious."

lessons.title: Reading a high route
lessons.objective: You can read contours to find a safer line.

payload.prompt: Contours merge into one thick line on the north face. A saddle sits to the south. Best line?

options.text: Use the saddle to cross the ridge and skip the merged contours
options.explanation: The saddle is a low, gentle point on the ridge. Merged contours mean a cliff, which you avoid.

options.text: Go straight up the north face since it is shortest
options.explanation: Merged contours signal near-vertical ground. The shortest line is not a safe line here.

options.text: Walk along the top edge of the cliff to look for a gap
options.explanation: Walking a cliff edge puts you right on the exposure. Look for the low, gentle crossing instead.

options.text: Pick whichever looks flattest on the phone screen
options.explanation: A screen picture cannot show slope. Read the contour spacing on the map instead.

explanation.correct: A saddle is the low point between two high points, where the ridge is gentlest to cross. Contours that merge mean cliffs, so the saddle bypass keeps you off steep ground.
explanation.incorrect: Merged contour lines mean a wall. A saddle, shown as an hourglass shape on the map, offers a lower, gentler way over the ridge.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I'd take the saddle. That north face is cliffs."

payload.prompt: Contours bend downhill, away from higher ground. Ridge or drainage?

scene.alt: A topographic map where a set of contour lines bulge outward toward lower ground like fingers pointing downhill.

explanation.correct: On a ridge or spur, contours bend downhill, away from higher ground. In a drainage they point uphill, toward the higher ground the water comes from.
explanation.incorrect: Contours that point downhill mark a ridge or spur. In a drainage, the V shapes point uphill, toward higher ground. Check the elevation numbers to be sure which way is up.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Those bend downhill. That's a ridge, not a gully."

payload.prompt: Two lines reach the same lake. Which one do you take?

situation.narrative: On your topo map, line A follows a rounded spur where contours are evenly spaced. Line B cuts straight up a slope where the contours are packed together and merge in two places before a saddle.

options.label: Take line A: longer, but the spacing shows steady, gentle ground
options.consequence: Even contour spacing means a consistent grade with no surprises, and it reaches the saddle. The extra distance is a fair trade for safety.
considerations: Wide, even spacing means gentle ground.
Merged contours are a warning about cliffs.

options.label: Start on line B and look for a break in the steep part
options.consequence: Checking is reasonable, but you would already be climbing toward the steepest ground. Be ready to turn around before you are committed.
considerations: Decide your turn-back point before you start.
Merged contours are hard to fix from below.

options.label: Take line B because straight lines save time
options.consequence: Packed and merged contours mean very steep ground or cliffs. Saving a few minutes is not worth the exposure for a tired group.
considerations: The shortest line is not always the safest.
Fatigue makes steep ground more dangerous.

options.label: Follow whichever direction looks like the most footprints
options.consequence: Footprints show where people went, not where it is safe. Some of those people may have been lost or off route.
considerations: Use the map to choose the line.
Confirm with what you can see on the ground.

payload.expertNote: Contour spacing is the safest quick read in the mountains: wide means gentle, tight means steep, merged means a wall. Choose the line that keeps you off the wall.
payload.sayThisLine: "Even contours on the spur. Let's take the long way and skip the wall."
payload.safetyNote: Carry a paper map and compass and know how to use them. Do not attempt cliffs or scrambles beyond your skills.

payload.prompt: Complete the contour rules for choosing a high route:
payload.template: Contours close together mean {{steep}} ground. Contours that merge mean a {{merge}}, and a saddle is a low point on a ridge.

explanation.correct: Tight spacing means steep ground, and merged lines mean cliffs. A saddle is the low, gentle crossing on a ridge, so it is often the safer line.
explanation.incorrect: Close contours mean steep terrain, and lines that merge mean a cliff. Look for a saddle to cross a ridge where it is lowest.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Tight lines mean steep. Merged lines mean cliffs."

lessons.title: Altitude and pacing
lessons.objective: You can pace and sleep sensibly at altitude.

payload.prompt: Above 10,000 ft, about how much should your sleeping elevation rise per night?

explanation.correct: Wilderness medicine guidance suggests raising your sleeping elevation by roughly 1,000 to 1,600 ft a night once you are above about 10,000 ft, with a rest day every few days.
explanation.incorrect: The common guidance is to raise your sleeping elevation by only about 1,000 to 1,600 ft per night above 10,000 ft. Slow, steady gains give your body time to adapt.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We're keeping the sleeping-altitude gains small."

payload.prompt: At 11,000 ft, your friend has a headache and nausea. What now?

situation.narrative: You drove up yesterday and are on a high-country day hike. Your friend says she has a pounding headache, feels sick to her stomach and is more tired than usual. The summit is still 1,200 ft above you.

options.label: Skip the summit and walk down together to lower elevation
options.consequence: Going lower is the most reliable fix for altitude sickness. Symptoms that get worse or are joined by confusion, stumbling or breathlessness at rest are an emergency.
considerations: Do not go higher with symptoms.
If she worsens or shows confusion or trouble breathing, descend and call for help.

options.label: Rest here, drink, eat, and stay at this elevation to see if she improves
options.consequence: Resting without going higher is reasonable for mild symptoms, if you watch her closely. Descend right away if she is not improving or gets worse.
considerations: Set a short time limit and then descend if there is no improvement.
Never sleep higher than where she is feeling well.

options.label: Push on to the summit quickly, then descend
options.consequence: Going higher with symptoms can make altitude illness worse and put you far from lower ground when she needs it.
considerations: Symptoms are a warning, not a challenge.
Summit fever can override good judgment.

options.label: Take a pain reliever and keep going as planned
options.consequence: Covering up symptoms does not fix the cause. A headache is your early signal that your body has not adapted to the elevation.
considerations: Treat the cause by staying put or descending.
Do not hide symptoms to keep the plan.

payload.expertNote: The safest rules are simple: do not go higher with symptoms, and go down if they worsen. Confusion, stumbling or breathlessness at rest mean descend now and get help.
payload.sayThisLine: "Headache and nausea up here. Let's go down and try again later."
payload.safetyNote: Follow WMS and park guidance. Descent is the treatment. If someone is confused, stumbling or short of breath at rest, descend and call for emergency help.

payload.prompt: Which sign at altitude means descend now and get help?

options.text: Confusion, stumbling, or breathlessness even at rest
options.explanation: These point to serious forms of altitude illness in the brain or lungs. They are emergencies.

options.text: Feeling a bit sleepy after lunch
options.explanation: Mild tiredness is common on any hike. It alone is not the red flag.

options.text: Being thirsty after a steep climb
options.explanation: Thirst is normal after effort. Drink and keep an eye on other signs.

options.text: Cold hands at a windy pass
options.explanation: Cold hands are a comfort and layering issue, not a sign of altitude illness.

explanation.correct: Confusion, stumbling, or breathlessness at rest signal severe altitude illness, such as HACE or HAPE. Descend immediately, get help, and do not leave the person alone.
explanation.incorrect: The red flags are confusion, trouble walking straight, or shortness of breath at rest. Descend right away and call for emergency help.
explanation.sayThisLine: "He's confused and stumbling. We go down now and call for help."

payload.prompt: Put a sensible altitude plan in order:

items.text: Arrive and spend a night or two at moderate elevation
items.why: Letting your body adjust before you climb high is the foundation of acclimatization.

items.text: Do a day hike higher, then come back down to sleep
items.why: Climb high, sleep low is a classic way to help your body adapt without a big jump in sleeping altitude.

items.text: Raise your sleeping elevation gradually on later nights
items.why: Small nightly gains give your body time to keep up as you go higher.

items.text: Take a rest day every few days above 10,000 ft
items.why: A rest day lets you adjust before the next push higher.

items.text: Save your biggest, highest day for when you feel fully well
items.why: Feeling good and well adapted makes the toughest day safer and more fun.

explanation.correct: Start moderate, climb high and sleep low, raise your sleeping elevation slowly, add rest days, and save the biggest day for when you feel well.
explanation.incorrect: Build up gradually: moderate elevation first, climb high and sleep low, small nightly gains, rest days, and the biggest day last, only if you feel well.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Climb high, sleep low, and take it slow."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: We spent two nights at nine thousand before going higher. My legs felt slow, but no headaches this time.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: Acclimatizing by spending time at moderate elevation first
options.explanation: Yes. Two nights at moderate elevation gave her body time to adapt, which helped avoid altitude sickness.

options.text: Bonking from running out of food
options.explanation: She did not mention food or energy running out. She linked slow legs and no headaches to time at elevation.

options.text: Starting before dawn to avoid storms
options.explanation: An alpine start is about timing the day, not adjusting to elevation over several nights.

options.text: Setting a turnaround time
options.explanation: A turnaround is a clock rule for a single day. She described how she spent multiple nights.

payload.translation: She let her body adapt to elevation by spending a couple of nights at moderate height before climbing higher, and she avoided altitude headaches.

followUps.line: Do you follow climb high, sleep low?
followUps.why: It shows you know a standard acclimatization strategy and invites her tips.

followUps.line: How high did you sleep on your last trip?
followUps.why: It is a friendly, specific question about her plan and pace.
